frame.objective: Determine whether FLIR Systems should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its uncooled thermal imaging cores, based on evidence available up to mid-2013.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-2013; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as market demand, technical feasibility, competitive landscape, and FLIR’s existing B2B focus.
Alternatives must include no expansion, a different route to consumers, a different customer group, or a product redesign.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home safety, outdoor recreation) using uncooled cores.
2) Expand B2B offerings by targeting new industrial or government segments with enhanced thermal capabilities.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing military, government, law enforcement, and industrial markets.
4) Change route to consumers by partnering with retailers or creating a direct-to-consumer e‑commerce model, leveraging existing core technology.
5) Target a different customer group (e.g., DIY enthusiasts, small businesses) with a differentiated proposition, using core technology as a base.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt thermal imaging cameras for outdoor recreation and home safety if the device is positioned as a premium, easy-to-use tool that provides real-time thermal imagery, because the perceived utility (e.g., detecting hidden heat sources) creates a willingness to pay a premium price.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts and homeowners seeking non-intrusive temperature detection for hunting, camping, fire safety, and home inspection.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The ability to 'see' heat energy changes the perceived risk and problem-solving capability, making the product feel like a high-value tool rather than a specialized industrial instrument.
T1.how_value_is_captured: FLIR can capture value through premium pricing (e.g., $1,195 for the i3) and direct-to-consumer sales, leveraging its existing core technology to differentiate from lower-cost alternatives.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for thermal imaging when it is marketed as a consumer-friendly product.
The uncooled core technology is sufficient for consumer use cases without compromising performance.
Retail distribution channels can reach the target audience effectively.
predictions: In a test offering the i3 to outdoor recreationists, at least 30% will express intent to purchase at a price point above $1,000.
Sales conversion rate will be higher among users who cite thermal imaging for hunting or home safety than for general outdoor activities.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt thermal imaging cameras for outdoor recreation and home safety if the device is positioned as a premium, easy-to-use tool that provides real-time thermal imagery, because the perceived utility (e.g., detecting hidden heat sources) creates a willingness to pay a premium price.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt thermal imaging cameras for home safety and DIY projects if the device is marketed as an affordable, easy-to-use tool for detecting electrical hazards, fire, and structural issues, because the perceived utility (e.g., identifying hidden electrical problems) creates a willingness to pay a lower premium price.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners and DIY electricians who need reliable, non-intrusive methods to detect electrical hazards and structural issues.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The ability to 'see' electrical currents and heat sources reduces perceived risk and allows for proactive maintenance, making the product feel like a practical, everyday tool rather than a specialized industrial instrument.
T2.how_value_is_captured: FLIR can capture value through lower price positioning (e.g., under $1,000) and retail distribution, leveraging its existing core technology to serve a new consumer segment.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a lower premium for thermal imaging when it is framed as a home safety and DIY tool.
The uncooled core technology is sufficient for consumer use cases without compromising safety or performance.
Retail channels can effectively reach homeowners and DIY users.
predictions: In a test offering the i3 to homeowners, at least 25% will express intent to purchase at a price point below $1,000.
Sales conversion will be higher among users who cite home safety and DIY projects than for general outdoor activities.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from 1983 public sources to justify Mag Instrument investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its machined anodized-aluminium flashlights.
constraints: Limited to public sources available before 1983; no internal company data.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, home safety) using the existing flashlight design.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line to include consumer‑grade variants without differentiation, selling through retail or online channels.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (police, firefighters, public safety).
4) License the flashlight design to third‑party manufacturers for consumer branding, capturing value through royalties.
5) Partner with a consumer brand to co‑develop and market a differentiated flashlight for a specific use case.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home gardeners that emphasizes water efficiency, convenience, and premium pricing, supported by evidence of drip irrigation's superior efficiency (90% vs. 50-70% for sprinkler) and Netafim's existing marketing for home use.

frame.objective: Determine whether Netafim should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its drip-irrigation technology, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited public information on Netafim’s current consumer reach and sales; evidence must be from sources available by mid-2025.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home gardeners, small urban farms) with a new product or service built on drip technology.
2) Expand existing B2B offerings to new segments or markets without creating a new consumer proposition (e.g., deeper integration with e‑commerce, new distribution channels).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B customers and existing product lines, avoiding new consumer initiatives.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: They will switch from manual watering or sprinkler systems to a drip kit because it promises higher water efficiency (90% vs. 50-70% for sprinkler) and lower maintenance, aligning with growing environmental and cost-awareness.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Netafim would capture value through premium pricing for a differentiated kit, higher margins from a niche consumer segment, and brand positioning as an efficient irrigation leader.

predictions: Surveyed home gardeners will indicate intent to purchase a drip kit at a price 20-30% above standard kits.

X1.name: Purchase Intent Test for Home Gardeners
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product pages and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 300 adult home gardeners (small to medium-sized gardens, 50% in the US, 50% in India) recruited via panel providers.
X1.measure: Percentage of respondents who indicate intent to purchase a differentiated drip kit at a price 20-30% above standard kits (WTP). Secondary measure: self-reported water usage frequency and time savings.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 45% of respondents will indicate intent to purchase a premium drip kit, with WTP above 20% above standard kits.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 45% of respondents will indicate intent to purchase a smart drip kit, with WTP above 30% above standard kits.

X1.decision_rule: If intent to purchase a premium drip kit (T1) exceeds 45% and its WTP exceeds 20% above standard kits, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If intent to purchase a smart drip kit (T2) exceeds 45% and its WTP exceeds 30% above standard kits, develop a smart-IoT proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into a consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address home gardeners' purchase intent or willingness to pay for a differentiated drip kit. Therefore it does not affect T1.

Participants are randomly assigned to either a price-only scenario (current price over €11,000) or an incentive-only scenario (same price but with a simulated €2,000 subsidy). They indicate likelihood to purchase and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 300 German homeowners (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel to match age, income, and solar awareness.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the price-only scenario.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the incentive-only scenario.

X1.decision_rule: If the incentive-only group shows at least 5% higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than the price-only group, adopt T2. If the price-only group shows at least 5% higher purchase intent and willingness to pay, adopt T1. If both differences are below 5%, no clear preference and further evidence is needed.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Evidence shows SMA residential storage is currently priced at over €11,000, making it unaffordable for most households. A test is needed to confirm whether price reduction below €2,000 would increase adoption.
final.target_customer: German homeowners with existing solar PV systems seeking energy independence and cost savings.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that lowers the effective price of residential storage through either reduced production costs or subsidy-driven affordability, enabling SMA to capture higher unit volume and potential premium pricing.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Price vs Incentive Test (300 homeowners, 6 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under price-only and incentive-only scenarios.

would_change_if: If the test shows the incentive-only group achieving at least 5% higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than the price-only group, T2 would become more likely and a subsidy-focused strategy would be considered.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available up to late 2009 to justify Martek Biosciences investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its algae-derived DHA omega-3 oil.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2009; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, regulatory feasibility, competitive landscape, and Martek’s existing B2B relationships.
Must consider Martek’s current B2B focus (infant formula, food/beverage/supplements) and any gaps in its current distribution channels.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., direct-to-consumer supplements, food ingredients, or a new consumer brand).
2) Expand B2B sales by targeting additional infant formula manufacturers or by offering the oil to other food/beverage/supplement segments without a differentiated consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on B2B sales and not pursue a consumer proposition.
4) Change the route to consumers by partnering with retailers or creating a direct-to-consumer e‑commerce channel, leveraging existing B2B distribution.
5) Target a different customer group (e.g., older adults, athletes, or pet owners) with a consumer proposition, using the same DHA oil base.

T1.claim: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a differentiated DHA supplement if they perceive it as a safe, natural alternative to fish oil, leading to higher willingness-to-pay and repeat purchases.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking omega-3s without fish exposure; Martek benefits through premium pricing and brand extension.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing consumer awareness of fish oil risks (e.g., mercury) and demand for plant-based nutrition drives preference for algae-derived DHA.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Martek can charge a premium for a branded consumer product and expand its life‑DHA line into new retail channels.
assumptions: Consumers are aware of DHA sources and safety concerns.
Regulatory approval for consumer claims is achievable by 2009.
Retail distribution can be secured without major infrastructure changes.
predictions: A survey of health-conscious adults will show >30% would purchase a branded DHA supplement at a price 20% above fish oil.
Sales of a new consumer product will exceed 10,000 units in the first year in a target retail channel.
T1.first_claim: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a differentiated DHA supplement if they perceive it as a safe, natural alternative to fish oil, leading to higher willingness-to-pay and repeat purchases.

T2.claim: Regulatory constraints will limit consumer adoption of DHA supplements in 2009, making a differentiated consumer proposition unviable.
T2.who_benefits: Regulatory bodies (EFSA, FDA) benefit by maintaining safety standards; Martek benefits if it can secure consumer claims.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: EFSA rejected Martek’s claim in 2009, indicating that consumer demand is constrained by unproven health benefits.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Martek would need to invest in B2B sales or alternative consumer channels to offset lost consumer revenue.
assumptions: Regulatory standards for DHA supplements are strict and unchanging by 2009.
Consumers will not switch to a branded supplement if regulatory approval is lacking.
Martek can adapt its product to meet new claims without major cost.
predictions: A survey of health-conscious adults will show <20% would purchase a branded DHA supplement due to regulatory concerns.
Sales of a new consumer product will not exceed 5,000 units in the first year despite marketing efforts.
T2.first_claim: Regulatory constraints will limit consumer adoption of DHA supplements in 2009, making a differentiated consumer proposition unviable.

assessments.quote: Awareness of the life'sDHA brand, after only two years in the marketplace, has more than doubled since 2007 from 11 to 28 percent among health-conscious consumers.
assessments.does_not_show: The source does not demonstrate that awareness translates into purchase intent or willingness-to-pay.

assessments.quote: At the end of last year, however, EFSA added Martek’s claim to its long list of rejections.
assessments.does_not_show: The source does not indicate whether the rejection was due to safety concerns, regulatory requirements, or other reasons, nor does it address consumer demand.

assessments.quote: The company said sales for the three months ended January 31 2009 were up 7 percent over last year to $84m, boosted particularly by infant formula customers outside the US.
assessments.does_not_show: The source does not explain why sales increased or whether it was driven by consumer demand versus B2B sales.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting diet‑drinks and snacks, emphasizing sugar‑free taste and calorie reduction. Begin with a limited launch of a branded consumer product and partner with existing B2B suppliers to test market response before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1981 to justify G.D. Searle investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its aspartame sweetener.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1981; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, regulatory status, and Searle’s existing B2B supply chain.
Cannot assume later developments; must rely on information known in 1981.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., diet soft drinks, weight‑management beverages, or functional foods).
2) Expand the existing B2B supply of aspartame to additional food and beverage manufacturers without a differentiated consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on prescription medicines and hospital supply.
4) Pursue a different route to consumers (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales, retail partnerships, or a subscription model) while retaining the aspartame product.
5) Target a different customer group (e.g., individual consumers, schools, or small businesses) with a differentiated proposition.

T1.claim: Individual consumers will adopt aspartame as a tabletop sweetener primarily because it eliminates sugar calories and offers a sugar‑free taste, leading them to purchase it for diet‑drinks and snacks.

arguments.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1981 to justify G.D. Searle investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its aspartame sweetener.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1981; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, regulatory status, and Searle’s existing B2B supply chain.
Cannot assume later developments; must rely on information known in 1981.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., diet soft drinks, weight‑management beverages, or functional foods).
2) Expand the existing B2B supply of aspartame to additional food and beverage manufacturers without a differentiated consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on prescription medicines and hospital supply.
4) Pursue a different route to consumers (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales, retail partnerships, or a subscription model) while retaining the aspartame product.
5) Target a different customer group (e.g., individual consumers, schools, or small businesses) with a differentiated proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether KONE should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings (elevators, escalators, moving walks, automatic doors, and lifecycle maintenance/modernization) for building owners and facility managers, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable path to capture value for KONE.
Any recommendation must consider KONE’s existing B2B relationships and indirect consumer reach.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home elevators, residential escalators, or consumer automatic doors).
2) Expand B2B services by deepening predictive maintenance or modernization offerings for building owners.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B markets and lifecycle services.
4) Change route to market: target individual buyers directly through e‑commerce or partnerships, bypassing building owners.
5) Target a different customer group: focus on developers, authorities, or other non‑building owners rather than facility managers.

T1.claim: Home elevators are a consumer convenience product, not a building owner service. If KONE offers a differentiated consumer proposition (e.g., a home elevator brand), individual buyers will purchase it directly, paying a premium for convenience and design, and KONE will capture value through brand sales and direct revenue.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and renters seeking convenient, stylish access to upper floors.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from relying on building owner services to owning a personal convenience product when they perceive it as a lifestyle item rather than a service requirement.
T1.how_value_is_captured: KONE sells a branded home elevator directly to consumers, earning premium margins on a differentiated product line.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a branded home elevator over standard building elevators.
KONE can design, manufacture, and market a consumer-grade home elevator within its existing capabilities.
Direct-to-consumer sales can be executed without significant infrastructure changes.
predictions: A survey of homeowners would show >30% would purchase a home elevator at a price 20% above standard building elevators.
Pilot sales of a consumer-branded home elevator would generate at least €50,000 in revenue within 12 weeks.
Consumers would cite convenience and design as primary purchase drivers, not cost or service contracts.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Alfa Laval investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a differentiated product.
Any recommendation must consider Alfa Laval’s existing B2B presence and current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home water filtration, small‑scale food processing, marine recreational equipment).
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio with new industrial features or services without creating a separate consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current industrial customers and existing B2B channels.
4) Partner with or license technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Alfa Laval brand.
5) Target a new customer segment (e.g., small‑to‑medium home‑care manufacturers) with a tailored offering.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium messaging arm will achieve WTP ≥ €50 and purchase intent ≥ 60% among homeowners; convenience messaging will achieve ≥ €40 WTP and ≥ 50% purchase intent.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience messaging arm will achieve WTP ≥ €40 and purchase intent ≥ 50% among homeowners; premium messaging will achieve ≥ €50 WTP and ≥ 60% purchase intent.

X1.decision_rule: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition only if both arms meet their respective thresholds (premium arm: WTP ≥ €50 and purchase intent ≥ 60%; convenience arm: WTP ≥ €40 and purchase intent ≥ 50%). arguments.measure: Average WTP in euros for a branded consumer product (e.g., a water filtration system) and self‑reported likelihood to purchase on a 7‑point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium messaging arm will achieve WTP ≥ €50 and purchase intent ≥ 60% among homeowners; convenience messaging will achieve ≥ €40 WTP and ≥ 50% purchase intent.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience messaging arm will achieve WTP ≥ €40 and purchase intent ≥ 50% among homeowners; premium messaging will achieve ≥ €50 WTP and ≥ 60% purchase intent.

arguments.decision_rule: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition only if both arms meet their respective thresholds (premium arm: WTP ≥ €50 and purchase intent ≥ 60%; convenience arm: WTP ≥ €40 and purchase intent ≥ 50%). If only one arm meets its threshold, do not invest; if neither meets, decline expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The existing B2B presence and current reach to individual buyers provide a foundation for future exploration.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Bausch & Lomb investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current portfolio of contact lenses, lens care solutions, OTC eye drops and vitamins, Rx eye drugs, diagnostics and surgical products.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.
Search budget of 8 keyword searches.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Bausch & Lomb’s existing B2B and B2C channels and its current reach to individual buyers.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility within the given constraints.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., a new line of contact lenses or eye care products marketed directly to consumers).
2) Expand the existing portfolio by adding new products or services without a differentiated consumer proposition (e.g., introducing a new OTC eye drop formulation).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B and B2C channels and not pursue a new consumer proposition.
4) Change the route to market or customer group (e.g., selling through new retail channels or targeting a different demographic) without altering the product.

assumptions: There is a measurable demand for a differentiated product in the identified use case.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that directly addresses their specific need.
Bausch & Lomb can develop and market the product effectively within its existing channels.
predictions: If a test offers a differentiated product for dry eyes to a target segment, purchase intent or actual purchases will be higher than for a generic OTC eye drop.
Surveyed participants will rank the dry eye benefit as a top reason for choosing the product.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners (DIY interest) and 250 manufacturers/workshops (small-scale automation). Randomly assign 250 each to see consumer or manufacturer messaging.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will show higher intent and WTP than manufacturers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Manufacturers will show higher intent and WTP than homeowners.

X1.decision_rule: If homeowners' intent rate exceeds manufacturers' by at least 10 percentage points and their WTP is at least 20% higher, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition. If manufacturers' intent rate exceeds homeowners' by at least 10 percentage points and their WTP is at least 20% higher, target manufacturers. If both rates are equal, no expansion is recommended.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Eppendorf investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Need to identify a specific use case with clear consumer need and Eppendorf’s ability to differentiate and capture value.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home DIY lab, small business, or a niche professional segment).
2) Expand into adjacent B2B segments with existing products (e.g., add new consumables or accessories to existing lab instrument lines).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on academic and industrial research labs.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct-to-consumer online sales, partnerships with retailers, or subscription model) without altering product offering.

T1.who_benefits: Home DIY users and small businesses seeking professional-grade lab tools for hobbyist or small-scale experiments.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing interest in home science, DIY biology, and small-scale research creates a demand for accessible, high-quality lab equipment that can be purchased without lab access.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Eppendorf would sell premium-priced instruments and consumables directly to consumers online, capturing margin through direct-to-consumer sales and brand positioning.

Regulatory compliance for consumer-grade lab equipment exists.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: The high cost and complexity of purchasing and maintaining professional lab equipment deter most consumers; a subscription or rental model lowers the barrier and makes ownership affordable.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Eppendorf would generate recurring revenue through subscription fees and rental charges, while also selling consumables at a premium, capturing value through recurring revenue and brand loyalty.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Ottobock investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable path to capture value from individual buyers.
Any recommendation must consider Ottobock’s existing B2B revenue streams and current consumer reach (400 patient care centres).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home use, fashion‑oriented prosthetics, or a new mobility solution) with a direct-to-consumer or partner channel.
2) Expand the existing B2B offerings by adding new features, services, or distribution channels without creating a separate consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B markets (clinics, technicians, distributors, payers, and patient care centres).
4) Partner with or license Ottobock technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than creating a proprietary consumer brand.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they view prosthetics and orthotics as a lifestyle or fashion item, leading to multiple purchases and premium pricing.
T1.who_benefits: Individual users seeking aesthetic and functional differentiation beyond clinical necessity.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Shifting perception from medical necessity to personal style and status increases willingness to buy multiple pairs and pay higher prices for design and brand.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Ottobock can capture value through direct-to-consumer sales, premium pricing, and brand licensing, leveraging its design expertise to create differentiated product lines.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to allocate discretionary spending on prosthetics and orthotics beyond clinical needs.
Aesthetic and fashion-driven demand can be measured and monetized through a consumer brand.
Ottobock can maintain quality and functionality while offering design differentiation.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate higher purchase intent for a fashion-oriented line compared to a functional-only line.
Willingness to pay for a differentiated design will be above the baseline price point for standard orthotics.
Repeat purchase rate for multiple pairs will be higher than for a single-use functional product.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they view prosthetics and orthotics as a lifestyle or fashion item, leading to multiple purchases and premium pricing.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive prosthetics and orthotics as a medical necessity, leading to repeat purchases for clinical use and lower willingness to pay for design differentiation.
T2.who_benefits: Clinicians, technicians, and payers who require reliable, functional devices for patient care.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Regulatory, insurance, and clinical requirements mandate specific features and performance standards, making design differentiation less attractive and increasing procurement costs.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Ottobock can capture value through volume sales to clinics, higher margins on standard products, and potential licensing of clinical-grade features to third parties.
assumptions: Clinical demand is driven by regulatory and insurance requirements rather than consumer style.
Design differentiation does not meet minimum functional standards required for clinical use.
Clinicians prioritize cost-effectiveness and compliance over aesthetic features.
predictions: Surveyed clinicians will indicate lower purchase intent for a fashion-oriented line compared to a functional-only line.
Willingness to pay for a differentiated design will be below the baseline price point for standard orthotics.
Repeat purchase rate for clinical use will be higher than for a single-use functional product.

assessments.quote: We help people maintain or regain their freedom of movement.
assessments.does_not_show: The statement does not address consumer perception of prosthetics as a lifestyle item or willingness to pay for design differentiation.

assessments.quote: Otto Bock sells its products only to those that are directly involved in clinical assessment and fitting of the product(s) to the patient/user, with the exception of Prosthetic and Orthotic schools.
assessments.does_not_show: The statement does not provide evidence that clinicians and payers prioritize clinical necessity over design differentiation; it only describes current sales channels.

X1.name: Consumer vs Clinical Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from two groups: a Consumer Group (n=200) and a Clinical Group (n=200). Each group views a product description of a standard orthotic device (identical specifications) presented in either a functional-only or a fashion-oriented framing. The Consumer Group also receives a follow-up offer to purchase a differentiated design line at a premium price. The test measures purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this product?") and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale.
X1.sample: 400 participants (200 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect Ottobock’s B2B market.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: purchase intent (binary) for the fashion-oriented line. Secondary outcomes: WTP (7-point scale) and repeat purchase intent (binary) for clinical use.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Consumer Group will show higher purchase intent and WTP for the fashion-oriented line than the Clinical Group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Clinical Group will show higher purchase intent and WTP for the functional-only line than the Consumer Group.

X1.decision_rule: If the Consumer Group’s purchase intent exceeds the Clinical Group’s by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 60% vs 50%), we conclude T1 is supported and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition. If the Clinical Group’s purchase intent exceeds the Consumer Group’s by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T2 is supported and recommend focusing on clinical B2B. If the difference is ≤ 10 percentage points, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer perception of prosthetics as a lifestyle item or willingness to pay for design differentiation. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence does not demonstrate consumer demand for a lifestyle or fashion-oriented line; Ottobock’s current B2B model and sales channels remain unchanged. Conduct a low‑cost test (e.g., the proposed Consumer vs Clinical Messaging Test) before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Individual users seeking aesthetic and functional differentiation beyond clinical necessity, currently served indirectly through Ottobock’s patient care centres.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer line that positions prosthetics and orthotics as lifestyle or fashion items, offering design variety, brand identity, and premium pricing while maintaining clinical quality.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Clinical Messaging Test (400 participants, 10‑week timeline, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a fashion-oriented line versus a functional-only line.
final.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay for design differentiation and the size of the market remain uncertain; the test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows the Consumer Group’s purchase intent for the fashion-oriented line exceeds the Clinical Group’s by at least 10 percentage points, we would shift to developing a differentiated consumer proposition.
If the test shows the Clinical Group’s purchase intent for the functional-only line exceeds the Consumer Group’s by at least 10 percentage points, we would focus on expanding clinical B2B offerings.
If neither group shows a meaningful difference, we would recommend no expansion and continue the current B2B model.

T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking reliable home automation solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If Phoenix Contact can demonstrate proven reliability and compatibility, homeowners will be more likely to purchase and integrate its products into their home automation systems.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Phoenix Contact can capture value by selling premium-priced, branded consumer products and potentially offering installation services or support.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for reliability and compatibility.
Phoenix Contact can communicate reliability through certifications, testing, and marketing.
The installation process is straightforward enough to be accessible to homeowners.
predictions: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent when presented with reliability certifications and compatibility information.
Sales of consumer-facing products will increase when reliability claims are highlighted in marketing.
Customers will report lower post-purchase support requests compared to competitors.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt Phoenix Contact products for home automation if they perceive the products as reliable, compatible with existing systems, and easy to install, because they value consistent performance and avoid compatibility issues.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt Phoenix Contact products for home automation if they perceive the products as a status symbol or premium lifestyle item, because they value brand prestige and are willing to pay for perceived quality and exclusivity.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking premium, high-end home automation solutions.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If Phoenix Contact can position its products as a status symbol, homeowners will be more likely to purchase them as a reflection of their lifestyle and financial status.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Phoenix Contact can capture value by offering premium-priced, branded consumer products and potentially limited-edition or exclusive designs.
assumptions: Homeowners associate premium branding with higher quality and reliability.
The target segment is willing to pay a premium for brand prestige.
Phoenix Contact can effectively communicate brand status through marketing and product positioning.
predictions: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent when presented with premium branding and limited-edition messaging.
Sales of consumer-facing products will increase when brand status is emphasized in marketing.
Customers will report higher satisfaction with the perceived prestige of the product.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Reliability vs. Status Messaging
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with random assignment to one of two product descriptions. Participants view a product description (e.g., a terminal block) and are asked to indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale. The two conditions are:
X1.sample: 300 homeowners (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home automation experience.
X1.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) and purchase intent (on a 7-point scale) for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the reliability condition compared to the status condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the status condition compared to the reliability condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP in the reliability condition exceeds the average WTP in the status condition by at least 1.5 points (e.g., 6.5 vs. 5.5 on a 7-point scale) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), then T1 is supported. If the status condition exceeds reliability by at least 1.5 points and the difference is statistically significant, then T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.

revisions.reason: The simulated result concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand, reliability perception, or willingness to pay for Phoenix Contact products. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home solar PV control) that emphasizes reliability, compatibility, and ease of installation. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test consumer demand and willingness to pay before scaling.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with existing or planned home solar PV systems who need control and protection for their inverters and associated equipment.
final.value_proposition: Phoenix Contact can offer a trusted, reliable solution for home solar PV control, leveraging its industrial expertise to provide durable, compatible components that reduce installation complexity and long-term support costs.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (300 homeowners, two product descriptions, willingness-to-pay and purchase intent) to validate demand for reliability-driven positioning.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for Phoenix Contact products and the specific willingness to pay for reliability are unknown. The test will clarify whether homeowners are willing to pay a premium for reliability.
would_change_if: If the test shows no significant difference between reliability and status messaging, or if willingness to pay is low, the recommendation would shift toward a different consumer proposition or no expansion.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for premium branding or status, the recommendation would shift toward a status-driven proposition.

arguments.objective: Determine whether Phoenix Contact should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial, energy, and infrastructure products, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current consumer reach and demand for Phoenix Contact products.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility of a differentiated proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home solar PV control, home air‑conditioning automation).
2) Expand the existing product portfolio into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑grade terminal blocks or small‑size power supplies).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on industrial, energy, and infrastructure customers.
4) Change the route to market for consumer products (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with retailers) without altering the product offering.

arguments.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Reliability vs. Status Messaging
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with random assignment to one of two product descriptions. Participants view a product description (e.g., a terminal block) and are asked to indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale. The two conditions are:
arguments.sample: 300 homeowners (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home automation experience.
arguments.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) and purchase intent (on a 7-point scale) for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the reliability condition compared to the status condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the status condition compared to the reliability condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP in the reliability condition exceeds the average WTP in the status condition by at least 1.5 points (e.g., 6.5 vs. 5.5 on a 7-point scale) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), then T1 is supported. If the status condition exceeds reliability by at least 1.5 points and the difference is statistically significant, then T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows Nordson already sells precision dispensing equipment to consumer and industrial markets, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or actual purchase behavior for home improvement projects. A limited test (e.g., purchase intent survey) is needed to validate whether consumers would adopt precision dispensing systems.

frame.objective: Determine whether Nordson should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B precision dispensing, coating, and X-ray inspection systems (EFD, ASYMTEK, Dage) for semiconductor, electronics, and industrial manufacturers.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any new proposition must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.
Investment decision must consider Nordson’s existing B2B market position and potential disruption to current revenue streams.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home improvement, automotive, or consumer packaging) with a new product or service model.
2) Expand the existing B2B offerings by adding new features, services, or distribution channels to serve semiconductor/electronics manufacturers without creating a separate consumer proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether Valmont should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B infrastructure and agriculture products, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., homeowner irrigation, outdoor lighting, or safety poles).
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio without a consumer focus (e.g., deeper service offerings, new distribution channels, or new product lines).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B infrastructure and agriculture markets.
4) Target a different customer group within the existing B2B base (e.g., small‑to‑medium‑size farms or urban utility companies) with a differentiated proposition.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they view irrigation and lighting as essential home improvements that improve property value and convenience, and they trust Valmont's reputation for durability and reliability.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking reliable outdoor lighting and irrigation solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If homeowners perceive these products as high-quality, long-lasting, and easy to install, they will be willing to purchase directly from a trusted brand rather than through traditional retailers.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Valmont can capture value by selling premium-priced, differentiated products directly to consumers through its own retail channels, earning higher margins than through its existing B2B distribution.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for durable, reliable outdoor lighting and irrigation equipment.
Valmont's brand reputation for quality and reliability translates into consumer trust.
Direct-to-consumer sales can be executed cost-effectively within the test budget.
predictions: A survey of homeowners will show a willingness to pay at least 20% more for a differentiated Valmont product compared to a comparable competitor.
Purchase intent will be higher for a product marketed as a premium, durable solution than for a standard product.
Sales conversion rate through a direct-to-consumer channel will exceed 5% of visitors.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they view irrigation and lighting as essential home improvements that improve property value and convenience, and they trust Valmont's reputation for durability and reliability.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they face increasing regulatory and safety requirements for outdoor lighting and irrigation, and they need products that meet these standards, making Valmont's compliance-focused offerings attractive.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners and property owners who must comply with local lighting and irrigation codes.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If homeowners perceive a product as compliant with safety and regulatory standards, they will be more likely to purchase it, even if it is priced higher, because they avoid potential fines or penalties for non-compliance.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Valmont can capture value by positioning its products as compliant and offering certification services, allowing it to charge a premium for safety-assured solutions.
assumptions: Local building codes and safety standards are increasingly strict for outdoor lighting and irrigation.
Homeowners are aware of these regulations and actively seek compliant products.
Valmont can easily communicate compliance credentials to consumers.
predictions: A survey of homeowners will show higher purchase intent for a product labeled as "code-compliant" compared to a standard product.
Sales of compliant products will be driven by regulatory awareness rather than price sensitivity.
The margin on compliant products will be higher than on standard products due to the premium price consumers are willing to pay for assurance.

X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase. Participants view two product descriptions of Victaulic flexible sprinkler fittings: one emphasizes safety and ease of installation (fire‑free, minimal disruption), and one emphasizes brand status and professional‑grade quality (premium, trusted by professionals). X1.sample: 300 homeowners (ages 25‑55) recruited via an online panel, balanced for geographic diversity and homeowner experience (DIY vs. professional).

constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.
